title: Easter Sunday
hookLine: the tomb is empty and the alleluia returns
last: THE WHOLE STORY IN ONE NIGHT.

cards: Since Ash Wednesday, a single word has been missing from the Mass. Not dropped by accident: put away. In some places, children even wrote it on a banner before Lent and buried it in the churchyard.
All through Lent the Gospel was greeted with other words. Then last night, after the readings, the priest sang it three times, each time a little higher, and the people sang it back.
This morning it's everywhere: on the doors, in the hymns, doubled at the end of Mass.

teach.h: TWO DISCIPLES RACE TO THE TOMB.
teach.b: Start with the morning Gospel. On Easter Sunday the Church reads John. Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb while it's still dark and finds the stone rolled away.
She runs to Peter and the other disciple, the one Jesus loved, and the two of them race back. The other disciple outruns Peter, gets there first, looks in, and waits.
Peter goes straight in and sees the linen cloths lying there, and the face cloth rolled up by itself.
Then the other disciple goes in, and John says he saw and believed. No angel's speech, no appearance yet. Just two out-of-breath men and an empty room.
Matthew puts it in an angel's mouth, in the Douay-Rheims: "He is not here, for he is risen, as he said." Now the word.

Alleluia is Hebrew: hallelu, praise, plural, all of you, and Yah, the short form of God's name. Praise the Lord, everybody. It opens and closes a run of Psalms, and the Book of Revelation has heaven singing it.

The Church buried it for Lent so that it could come back like this. Today the dismissal at the end of Mass gets a double alleluia, and it will keep it through the eight days of the octave and again at Pentecost.

teach.h: HE IS NOT HERE, FOR HE IS RISEN.
teach.b: Some Catholics also use a greeting from the Christian East this morning: one person says Christ is risen, and the other answers, he is risen indeed.
Christians say the tomb was empty because he was raised, and Paul writes that if Christ is not risen, their preaching is in vain. A great deal rests on that empty room.

how: On Easter Sunday Catholics celebrate Mass with the Gospel of the empty tomb, sing the alleluia that was silent through Lent, end Mass with a double alleluia, and often greet each other with Christ is risen and the answer he is risen indeed.

o: the morning of the empty tomb, when alleluia returns
the day the Spirit came down on the apostles
the Sunday Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey

s: in John's Easter Gospel, an angel greets Peter at the tomb
no angel speaks there: Peter finds the linen cloths, and the face cloth rolled up apart.
hallelu, praise, and Yah, God's name: praise the Lord.
in John's Easter Gospel, Peter reaches the tomb first
the other disciple outruns him and waits; Peter goes in first.

games.q: you're the other disciple, the one Jesus loved. you've outrun Peter to the tomb, and the stone is rolled away. what do you do?
o: run back to tell the others.
games.why: he looks in and waits. Peter arrives and goes straight in; then the other disciple goes in, and saw, and believed.

practice: Picture someone to tell, a parent, a friend, someone at Mass, a group chat, and say it to them quietly in whatever words fit: Christ is risen, or happy Easter, or simply alleluia.
If those aren't your words, picture the women running from the tomb, and notice what good news does to a body.

wordCard.voice: Easter Sunday. The morning of the empty tomb, when the alleluia comes back after Lent. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: praise Yah, praise the Lord — the word put away for Lent and sung again at Easter.

carryVoice: Your line: alleluia. Praise the Lord, everybody, sung again after the long quiet of Lent. Happy Easter.

sources.q: He is not here, for he is risen, as he said.
